ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

An infected ischemic limb

An ischemic foot that had been dry and sharply demarcated becomes swollen and foul-smelling. Purulent drainage appears, and biopsy now shows marked enzymatic tissue breakdown with numerous bacteria. Which additional process explains the transition?

  1. Conversion of calcium salts to triglycerides
  2. Sterile caseation without inflammation
  3. Bacterial infection with enzymatic liquefaction
  4. Restoration of normal epithelial differentiation
  5. Isolated hypertrophy of surviving muscle
Answer and explanation

Bacterial infection with enzymatic liquefaction

Superimposed infection adds leukocyte- and bacterial-enzyme-mediated digestion to ischemic tissue death, producing wet gangrene.

Option explanations

Bacterial infection with enzymatic liquefaction: Superimposed infection adds leukocyte- and bacterial-enzyme-mediated digestion to ischemic tissue death, producing wet gangrene.

Restoration of normal epithelial differentiation: Normal differentiation cannot explain purulence and malodor.

Isolated hypertrophy of surviving muscle: Hypertrophy does not explain infected necrotic tissue.

Conversion of calcium salts to triglycerides: Fat and calcium chemistry does not account for this clinical transition.

Sterile caseation without inflammation: Purulence indicates an inflammatory infectious process rather than sterile caseation.
